repos.name: meta / astryx
repos.description: An open source design system that's fully customizable and agent ready

summary.goal: Astryx is an open source design system built on React 19+ and StyleX, currently in Beta. It reportedly originated inside Meta over eight years and powers 13,000+ internal apps, providing 150+ accessible components, theming, dark mode, templates, and a CLI as one cohesive system.
summary.usage: Install via `npm install @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex` along with peer dependencies `react` and `react-dom` (React 19 or later required). The CLI can also be installed globally with `npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli`. Setup only needs CSS imports and a theme provider, with no build plugin, PostCSS, or Babel configuration.
summary.pros: Components are described as having open internals composable at any level, with a swizzle mechanism to eject a component's full source. Astryx states there is no styling lock-in, so StyleX-authored styles can be overridden via className using Tailwind, CSS modules, or plain CSS. It also ships seven ready-made themes.
summary.cons: Astryx is explicitly labeled as Beta, which may imply its API or behavior could still change. It also requires React 19 or later as a peer dependency, potentially limiting adoption on older React versions. Packages like @astryxdesign/vega and @astryxdesign/charts are published only under a @canary tag, with no stable release yet.
summary.fit: Astryx appears suited for React 19+ projects wanting a comprehensive, prebuilt design system without adopting StyleX directly, since styling can be overridden with a team's own tooling. It may be less suitable for teams on older React versions or needing stable chart/visualization components, given the canary-only status of those packages.

repos.name: ZhuLinsen / daily_stock_analysis
repos.description: LLM 驱动的多市场股票智能分析系统：多源行情、实时新闻、决策看板与自动推送，支持零成本定时运行。  LLM-powered multi-market stock analysis system with multi-source market data, real-time news, decision dashboard, automated notifications, and cost-free scheduled runs.

summary.goal: Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embeds web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into coding agents, steering them away from legacy JavaScript patterns toward native modern web platform solutions.
summary.usage: Install via `npx modern-web-guidance@latest install`, which runs an interactive setup wizard. The CLI also exposes `search`, `retrieve`, and `legacy-scan` subcommands to query guides or scan a codebase for legacy patterns without installing.
summary.pros: The project documents coverage of 250 modern web features and 203 real-world developer use cases spanning CSS, HTML, JavaScript, forms, security, performance, and accessibility. Guides are also described as token-efficient, since eval results are used to prune content that models already know.
summary.cons: By default, the tool collects anonymous usage telemetry (installation counts, retrieval IDs, search queries), which teams with strict data-handling policies may need to review or disable via the `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` environment variable before adoption.
summary.fit: This appears best suited for teams integrating AI coding agents (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity) into web development workflows, where guidance covering CSS, JavaScript, forms, security, and performance could help reduce legacy pattern usage, though the README does not state a recommended team size or project scale.

repos.name: shadcn / improve
repos.description: Use your most capable model to audit your codebase and write plans for cheaper models to execute.

summary.goal: improve is an agent skill that audits any codebase and writes implementation plans for other agents to execute. It is designed so a capable model handles understanding and judgment while a cheaper model executes; the skill itself never implements changes — the plan is the stated deliverable.
summary.usage: Install with `npx skills add shadcn/improve` in an agent that supports the Agent Skills format. Run `/improve` for a full audit producing prioritized findings and plans, or use variants such as `/improve quick`, `/improve security`, `/improve plan <description>`, and `/improve execute <plan>`, which dispatches a cheaper executor model and reviews its work.
summary.pros: Each finding is re-verified by re-reading the cited file:line location before being shown, which the README says reduces false positives. Generated plans are self-contained, include command-based verification gates, and define explicit STOP conditions for a smaller executor model. The skill only writes to the plans/ directory and never edits source code directly, leaving merging under the user's control.
summary.cons: Using the skill depends on an agent environment that supports the Agent Skills format, which may constrain which tools it works with (inferred). Even when `/improve execute <plan>` succeeds, the README states merging the resulting changes always remains a manual step for the user, so the workflow is not fully automated end to end.
summary.fit: The project fits workflows that pair one higher-cost advisory model with separate cheaper execution models through self-contained markdown plans. It is likely best suited to users already working within agents compatible with the Agent Skills format rather than standalone use (inferred).

repos.name: addyosmani / agent-skills
repos.description: Production-grade engineering skills for AI coding agents.

summary.goal: Agent Skills is a repository of production-grade engineering workflows for AI coding agents, packaging 25 skills (24 lifecycle skills plus a meta-skill) that encode practices such as spec-driven development, testing, review, and shipping across 9 slash commands.
summary.usage: Install all skills via the open skills CLI with `npx skills add addyosmani/agent-skills`, or install a single skill with `npx skills add addyosmani/agent-skills --skill <name>`. Native integrations are documented for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Codex, and other hosts.
summary.pros: The pack maps the development lifecycle to 9 slash commands that auto-activate relevant skills, includes 4 specialist agent personas, and bakes in documented engineering references such as Hyrum's Law and the test pyramid, which may improve consistency across agent-driven workflows.
summary.cons: A per-skill `npx` install copies only the single skill directory and not the shared `references/` directory, so supplementary checklists become unavailable unless the user clones the whole repo or copies files manually — a gap tracked as issue #361.
summary.fit: This project likely suits teams standardizing AI coding agent behavior across the software lifecycle, particularly those already using Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or similar supported hosts, given the documented native integrations for each.

repos.name: vercel-labs / agent-browser
repos.description: Browser automation CLI for AI agents

summary.goal: agent-browser is a native Rust command-line tool that gives AI agents browser automation: it opens pages, reads them as an accessibility-style tree, and lets the agent act on elements from the shell. The core loop uses `snapshot`, which returns the page as compact text with a ref (e.g. `@e1`) per element; the agent acts on a ref, then re-snapshots to check the result.
summary.usage: Install with `npm install -g agent-browser`, then run `agent-browser install` once to download Chrome for Testing. A documented quick start is: `agent-browser open example.com`, `agent-browser snapshot -i`, `agent-browser click @e1`, `agent-browser get url`, and `agent-browser close`.
summary.pros: Beyond refs, the CLI also supports CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators (e.g. `find role button`). It can drive multiple browser engines (Chrome for Testing by default, Lightpanda, Obscura) and cloud providers (Browserbase, Browserless, Browser Use, Kernel, AgentCore), and ships native binaries for macOS, Linux, and Windows.
summary.cons: A click is reported as failed rather than succeeding when the target element is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element (e.g. a consent banner), requiring the agent to dismiss the obstruction and take a new snapshot before retrying. Building from source also requires Node.js 24 or later, pnpm 11 or later, and Rust.
summary.fit: Given its stdio MCP server (`agent-browser mcp`) and documented integration guidance for Next.js/Vercel and eve agents, it appears aimed at AI-agent-driven browser automation pipelines, though teams without a Node/Rust toolchain may find source builds less convenient.

repos.name: we-promise / sure
repos.description: The personal finance app for everyone (by everyone)

summary.goal: Sure is a personal finance application and community-maintained fork of the discontinued Maybe Finance project, offering self-hosted tracking of cashflow, net worth, and spending.
summary.usage: Sure can be self-hosted via Docker or run locally for development: run `cp .env.local.example .env.local`, `bin/setup`, and `bin/dev`, then visit http://localhost:3000; optional demo data can be loaded with `rake demo_data:default`.
summary.pros: It supports access from a browser, macOS desktop app, mobile app, API clients, and LLM agents, and offers multiple one-click deployment options including Render, PikaPods, and Hostim, all under the AGPLv3 open-source license.
summary.cons: Local development requires specific prerequisites — a Ruby version matching `.ruby-version`, PostgreSQL newer than 9.3, and Redis newer than 5.4 — and the project maintains a public dashboard tracking known performance issues on data-heavy requests.
summary.fit: Given its AGPLv3 licensing and the explicit restriction against using the "Maybe" trademark in forks, Sure likely suits individuals or communities wanting a self-hosted, community-driven personal finance tool rather than an officially branded product.

repos.name: homeassistant-ai / ha-mcp
repos.description: Configure and automate Home Assistant with Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI assistants.

summary.goal: ha-mcp is a Model Context Protocol server letting AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT configure, automate, and manage a Home Assistant smart-home installation, going beyond basic voice-style device control to building automations, scripts, and dashboards.
summary.usage: The documented quick path installs the HA-MCP integration through HACS or the Home Assistant Marketplace (Home Assistant 2026.8.0 or newer), creates an administrator token, and points an AI client at the generated URL. Alternative server modes include Docker (`ghcr.io/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp`) and `uvx ha-mcp@latest` for Container/Core installs.
summary.pros: The README lists 87 tools spanning search, device control, automation/script/dashboard management, history/monitoring, and backups. Compared with Home Assistant's built-in MCP Server integration, ha-mcp documents a broader entity scope and added capabilities such as creating automations, editing dashboards, and managing backups, apps, and the device/entity registry.
summary.cons: File and YAML editing tools require opt-in beta feature flags (a master `ENABLE_BETA_FEATURES` flag plus sub-flags). The stdio transport is documented as having known connection issues (#1713) and is recommended only for demo/testing, not production use. The integration path requires Home Assistant 2026.8.0 or newer.
summary.fit: Per the documented comparison, ha-mcp may suit users wanting an AI assistant that builds and maintains Home Assistant configuration, not merely controls already-exposed devices, for which the built-in MCP Server integration is suggested instead. The app (add-on) path is described as best suited to Home Assistant OS/Supervised installs, while Container/Core setups appear to need Docker, PyPI, or stdio alternatives.

repos.name: openai / codex-security
repos.description: OpenAI's Codex Security CLI and TypeScript SDK for finding, validating, and fixing security vulnerabilities. npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@openai/codex-security

summary.goal: Codex Security is a workflow and tool for finding, investigating, and fixing vulnerabilities in code, usable within Codex sessions or automated via the `@openai/codex-security` CLI and TypeScript SDK.
summary.usage: Install the CLI globally with `npm install --global @openai/codex-security`, sign in using `cs login`, then run `cs scan .` from a repository directory to start a scan; results are saved as a Markdown report.
summary.pros: Features include scanning repositories, selected paths, or Git diffs, validating findings and generating patches, drafting SECURITY.md policies, tracking findings in Linear/Jira/GitHub, and exporting SARIF, JSON, or CSV reports.
summary.cons: The CLI requires Node.js 22.13.0+ (within the 22.x line) or Node.js 24.x/26.x, plus Python 3.10+, and Python 3.10 additionally requires the `tomli` package — a version mismatch could likely block installation.
summary.fit: This tool appears suited for teams wanting automated, CI-integrable vulnerability scanning across one or more repositories, with optional cloud-based findings review; local scans work without the cloud connection.

repos.name: TheAlgorithms / Java
repos.description: All Algorithms implemented in Java

summary.goal: The Algorithms - Java repository implements a collection of algorithms in Java, explicitly stated to be for educational purposes rather than production use.
summary.usage: Opening the Gitpod link at https://gitpod.io/#https://github.com/TheAlgorithms/Java launches a free online environment where the algorithms can be run and edited with a single click, and DIRECTORY.md lists the full set of implemented algorithms.
summary.pros: It offers a one-click Gitpod setup for experimenting without local installation, and maintains a DIRECTORY.md index covering the full set of implemented algorithms.
summary.cons: The README states these implementations may be less efficient than the Java standard library, since they are written for learning rather than optimized production use.
summary.fit: This appears best suited for students or developers studying algorithm implementations in Java, and those wishing to contribute should likely review CONTRIBUTING.md first.

repos.name: NVIDIA / auto-ontology
repos.description: Auto Ontology is a Python framework for building semantic, graph-based reasoning layers over data. It enables deterministic query generation, better context retrieval, and more explainable AI for LLM and agent workflows.

summary.goal: NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds a context layer over enterprise metadata so AI agents know where data lives, what it means, and whether and how to use it. It reconciles definitions across systems and exposes the ontology to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API, complementing semantic models an organization already owns.
summary.usage: Quickstart requires Docker with Compose v2, uv, and an NVIDIA API key from build.nvidia.com. Clone and configure the project with `git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology`, edit `.env`, then start the stack with `docker compose up -d --build`. The web UI runs on http://localhost:3000, where users sign in, enable Semantic Compilation, and ask questions in Chat.
summary.pros: Key features include natural-language querying translated to SQL, a semantic catalog/ontology layer stored in Postgres with pgvector, authentication and RBAC via Better Auth, a Web UI for chat, analysis, catalog, and settings, and flexible deployment via Helm chart or Docker Compose. It connects to ten database engines, including PostgreSQL, MySQL, Databricks, Snowflake, and DuckDB.
summary.cons: Although licensed under the Apache License 2.0, the project currently does not accept external contributions, limiting community-driven fixes or features to issue reports. Routing predictive questions to the optional KumoRFM service uploads connected table data to that hosted provider, so teams must review what is sent before enabling it.
summary.fit: Based on its Docker Compose and Helm deployment model and its NVIDIA API key requirement, Auto Ontology appears aimed at teams with existing enterprise databases and some infrastructure capacity rather than a zero-setup consumer tool. It likely suits organizations wanting an agent-facing semantic layer on top of relational data they already govern.

repos.name: anthropics / skills
repos.description: Public repository for Agent Skills

summary.goal: This repository provides Anthropic's reference implementation of Skills for Claude — folders containing instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude loads dynamically to perform specialized tasks such as document creation, data analysis, or workflow automation.
summary.usage: Skills can be installed in Claude Code as a plugin marketplace via `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills`, followed by `/plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills` or `/plugin install example-skills@anthropic-agent-skills`. They are also available directly to paid Claude.ai plans and through the Claude API.
summary.pros: Many skills, including the docx, pdf, pptx, and xlsx document-handling skills that power Claude's document capabilities in production, are released under the Apache 2.0 open-source license, giving developers reusable examples of complex, actively used skills.
summary.cons: The README states these skills are provided for demonstration and educational purposes only, and that actual Claude behavior may differ from what is shown, so users are advised to test skills thoroughly in their own environment before relying on them for critical tasks.
summary.fit: This project appears best suited for developers seeking patterns and inspiration for building their own Claude skills rather than for teams needing a guaranteed production-ready toolset out of the box.

repos.name: vercel-labs / agent-desktop
repos.description: Computer use CLI for AI agents

summary.goal: agent-desktop (vercel-labs) gives AI agents computer-use access to desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux by reading the OS accessibility tree as JSON, without screenshots or pixel matching. The agent loop (click/type on a ref, re-read, repeat) lives in the caller's code; agent-desktop itself contains no model. It ships as a CLI and a C library.
summary.usage: Install with `npm install -g agent-desktop`, then take an interactive snapshot with `agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i` and act on a returned ref with `agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8`. Bun, Yarn, pnpm, and Homebrew (macOS/Linux) can also install it; native archives are on GitHub Releases. It also supports an MCP server mode (`agent-desktop mcp`) exposing commands as tools.
summary.pros: Avoids screenshot/pixel-based automation by using structured accessibility-tree JSON with stable refs per snapshot, reducing brittleness to UI appearance changes. It offers 61 command names (57 operational) covering observation, input, window management, clipboard, and sessions, plus a C library (`libagent_desktop_ffi`) for in-process use.
summary.cons: Refs are scoped to a specific snapshot, so a stale or bare ref triggers errors like `INVALID_ARGS` or `STALE_REF`, requiring a fresh snapshot after UI changes. There is apparently no official Scoop package, and the project seemingly no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket, which may limit install options on some setups.
summary.fit: This tool seems best suited for developers building AI agents that need to observe and control native desktop applications programmatically, rather than web-only automation. Platform requirements appear fairly specific (macOS 13+, Windows 10 1809+, Ubuntu 24.04+), so compatibility with older OS versions is likely limited.

repos.name: milind-soni / OpenMausBot
repos.description: Open-source Grok Bot alternative with a virtual machine that bots can use

summary.goal: OpenMausBot is an open-source, Apache License 2.0 desktop chat app where each contact is an AI agent run locally via the `claude`, `codex`, or `grok` CLI, positioned as an open alternative to Grok Bot, Meta Muse, OpenAI dots, and Cue by Manus.
summary.usage: Released builds for macOS, Windows, and Ubuntu 24.04 embed the harness server. From source: `git clone https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot && cd OpenMausBot`, then `pnpm install` and `pnpm dev:server`/`pnpm dev`. Or run `npm install -g openmausbot` then `openmausbot`. Requires Node 24+ and a logged-in agent CLI.
summary.pros: It is local-first — a harness server on 127.0.0.1 stores transcripts and keys in `~/.openmausbot` rather than a vendor cloud. Risky actions need inline Allow/Deny approval. Bots can reach 500+ apps via Composio, and the project is free and open source.
summary.cons: Ubuntu support is beta, with Wayland host control disabled pending issue #345. The Windows installer is not yet code-signed, so SmartScreen flags it as an unknown publisher requiring 'Run anyway'.
summary.fit: OpenMausBot likely suits users who already hold a claude, codex, or grok CLI login wanting a local multi-agent chat app; it may fit less well for those needing fully hosted or mobile-first access, since that connectivity is still being built.

repos.name: cloudflare / security-audit-skill
repos.description: A coding-agent skill for multi-phase security audits with independently verified, machine-readable findings

summary.goal: security-audit is a skill that turns a coding agent into a security auditor, running audits through six phases: reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting. It is the single-repo starting point from which Cloudflare's multi-stage vulnerability discovery harness evolved.
summary.usage: Install via the Skills CLI with `npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill --skill security-audit` (add `--global` for a user-level install). Inside the codebase to audit, ask the coding agent to run a request such as `security audit this codebase`; an unspecified output directory defaults to `~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>`.
summary.pros: The workflow uses adversarial validation, where the agent that verifies a finding is never the one that found it, and produces three distinct verdicts (confirmed, needs_validation, rejected) validated against a schema. Cloudflare's test runs reportedly found a single run caught roughly half the vulnerabilities that repeated runs found in total, since ledgers and findings are additive across runs.
summary.cons: Executing target code (builds, tests, fuzzers) requires an OS-enforced sandbox that disables external networking, uses a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforces resource limits, and restricts writes to scratch paths; without it, leads reportedly stay marked needs_validation rather than being executed. This suggests full use of the skill may be difficult without existing sandbox infrastructure.
summary.fit: Given the sandboxing, Node.js, and parallel-sub-agent model requirements, the skill seems best suited to teams already using capable coding agents and willing to invest in isolated execution environments, rather than serving as a lightweight, drop-in audit tool.

repos.name: mattpocock / skills
repos.description: Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory.

summary.goal: This repository collects 'agent skills' aimed at structured, disciplined software engineering with AI coding agents, as an alternative to unstructured 'vibe coding.' The author describes the skills as small, easy to adapt, composable, and usable with any model, addressing recurring problems such as miscommunication with the agent, overly verbose output, non-working code, and codebases that degrade into unmanageable complexity.
summary.usage: Installation differs by agent: for Claude Code, run `claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@claude-plugins-official`; Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI each have their own install commands, and other agents can use `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills`, as listed under the 'Installation (30-second setup)' section and the skills.sh page at https://skills.sh/mattpocock/skills. After installing, run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` once per repository to configure the issue tracker, triage labels, and documentation location.
summary.pros: The skills are described as small, easy to adapt, composable, and model-agnostic. They bundle concrete practices such as 'grilling' sessions to align agent and user expectations, a shared glossary to reduce verbosity, a red-green-refactor TDD workflow, and a codebase-architecture scan that surfaces design-improvement candidates.
summary.cons: Users installing via a plugin (which updates automatically) versus the skills.sh editable-file method (updated by hand) should pick only one per agent, since installing both results in every skill being duplicated.
summary.fit: Based on its description, this project appears best suited to engineers already working with supported coding agents — Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, or others added via the generic installer — who want repeatable engineering discipline rather than unstructured AI-assisted coding.

repos.name: D4Vinci / Scrapling
repos.description: 🕷️ The BEST Web Scraping framework that handles everything from a single request to a full-scale crawl! Don't be shy, join here: https://discord.gg/EMgGbDceNQ and follow here for daily tips and tricks: https://x.com/Scrapling_dev

summary.goal: Scrapling is a Python web scraping framework that combines fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, DOM parsing/selection (CSS, XPath, text, regex), and concurrent crawling via a Scrapy-like Spider API in a single library. It supports extracting data from static pages, rendering JavaScript, interacting with sites, and capturing background API calls.
summary.usage: Install the core library with `pip install scrapling` (requires Python 3.10+). Browser-based fetchers need extra dependencies installed via `pip install "scrapling[fetchers]"` followed by `scrapling install` to download browsers. A minimal example fetches a page with `Fetcher.get()` and extracts data with CSS selectors like `.css('.quote .text::text').getall()`.
summary.pros: The README reports Scrapling's parser as roughly on par with or faster than Parsel/Scrapy and markedly faster than libraries like PyQuery, Selectolax, MechanicalSoup, and BeautifulSoup in text-extraction benchmarks. It also lists an MCP server for AI agent integration, a Spider framework with proxy rotation, pause/resume, and multiple export formats (JSON/JSONL/CSV/XML).
summary.cons: The base `pip install scrapling` only installs the parser engine; using fetchers or spiders requires installing the `[fetchers]` extra and running `scrapling install` to download browsers, otherwise a `ModuleNotFoundError` is raised. The project also requires Python 3.10 or higher.
summary.fit: Based on its documented feature set, Scrapling appears suited to Python developers who need a single tool spanning simple HTTP scraping, JavaScript-heavy sites, and larger crawling projects, including AI-agent-driven scraping through its MCP server. Teams needing strictly lightweight parsing-only usage may only need the base install.

repos.name: zed-industries / zed
repos.description: Code at the speed of thought – Zed is a high-performance, multiplayer code editor from the creators of Atom and Tree-sitter.

repos.name: Donchitos / Claude-Code-Game-Studios
repos.description: Turn Claude Code into a full game dev studio — 49 AI agents, 72 workflow skills, and a complete coordination system mirroring real studio hierarchy.

summary.goal: Claude Code Game Studios is a template repository for Claude Code that turns a described game idea into a one-page brief (design/game-brief.md) and a playable browser prototype (prototypes/<name>/), which can then be iterated on, grown into a full web/engine project, and eventually finished.
summary.usage: Clone the template with `git clone https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios.git my-game`, open the project root in Claude Code with `claude`, then type `/prototype` followed by a game idea to start the question-and-build workflow.
summary.pros: The template bundles 49 specialized agents, 75 skills/slash commands, and 62 document templates covering design, programming, art, QA, and production, with support for Web, Godot 4, Unity, and Unreal Engine 5 engines, and is released under the MIT License.
summary.cons: Several checks depend on optional tools: without Python 3, settings silently fall back to defaults, and without Chrome, Edge, or Chromium the prototype's play/screenshot checks are marked 'not assessed'; on Windows, Bash (via Git for Windows) is also required or hooks are skipped.
summary.fit: It appears suited to solo developers or small teams who want to start from a lightweight, question-driven prototyping workflow and optionally scale up to a heavier 'studio mode' for larger projects, though the finished games themselves are not shipped in the repository, only the template.

repos.name: google / skills
repos.description: Agent Skills for Google products and technologies

summary.goal: google/skills is a repository of "Agent Skills" for Google products and technologies, including Google Cloud, covering areas such as AI/ML, infrastructure, databases, security, developer tools, and advertising.
summary.usage: Skills are installed by running `npx skills add google/skills` and selecting which skills, target agents, and installation scope (project or global) to configure; `npx skills update` updates previously installed skills and optionally removes obsolete ones. Node.js is required if npx/npm are not already available.
summary.pros: The repository bundles a very large number of ready-made skills across many Google Cloud domains (GKE, BigQuery, IAM, Cloud Monitoring, etc.), plus plugin support for agent harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity CLI, reducing setup effort for agent-based workflows.
summary.cons: Users without Node.js must install it separately before running the npx-based installer, since the README states npx/npm/npx all come from that single dependency; the breadth of skills also implies users must select the specific subset relevant to their project rather than a single unified tool.
summary.fit: This project likely suits teams building AI agents that interact with Google Cloud services and want prepackaged, maintainable skill definitions rather than writing integration logic from scratch, though exact skill behavior details are not elaborated in the README.

repos.name: google-deepmind / mujoco
repos.description: Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact. A general purpose physics simulator.

summary.goal: MuJoCo (Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact) is a general-purpose physics engine designed to support research and development in robotics, biomechanics, graphics and animation, and machine learning, focusing on fast and accurate simulation of articulated structures interacting with their environment. It is maintained by Google DeepMind.
summary.usage: MuJoCo provides a C API along with Python bindings. The native Python package can be installed via `pip install mujoco` (requires Python >= 3.11). Prebuilt binaries for Linux, Windows, and macOS are also available from the GitHub releases page, which the documentation recommends as the primary installation method.
summary.pros: The runtime module is tuned for performance and operates on preallocated low-level data structures. It includes interactive visualization in both native desktop windows and web browsers, plus a wide ecosystem of first- and third-party bindings (Python, JavaScript/WebAssembly, C#/Unity, Swift, Java, Julia, Rust) and model converters (OpenSim, SDFormat, OBJ, Onshape).
summary.cons: Building from source is documented as an alternative to prebuilt binaries, but the tip of the `main` branch may be unstable. Prebuilt Linux wheels target the `manylinux2014` standard, which may limit compatibility with some older or non-standard distributions.
summary.fit: MuJoCo appears well suited for researchers and developers needing high-performance articulated-body simulation, though the README notes it is not an officially supported Google product, suggesting production use may warrant additional caution.

repos.name: herdrdev / herdr
repos.description: the runtime your coding agents live on

summary.goal: herdr is a terminal-based tool described as "the runtime your coding agents live on": it provides a background server that keeps agent terminal sessions running even when the client window closes or an SSH connection drops.
summary.usage: Install with `curl -fsSL https://herdr.dev/install.sh | sh` (brew, mise, or a Windows PowerShell script are also offered), then start it by running `herdr`. Detach from a session with `ctrl+b q` and reattach by running `herdr` again.
summary.pros: Sessions stay alive after disconnects, local work and saved SSH machines appear combined in one window, each pane is labeled working/blocked/idle, a CLI and socket API give agent-native control, and it ships as a single Rust binary without Electron.
summary.cons: After a server or machine restart, herdr restores the saved layout and can resume supported agent sessions, but the original processes themselves do not survive the restart.
summary.fit: The tool appears best suited to developers running command-line coding agents (e.g., Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, opencode, Grok) across one or more machines who want persistent, agent-aware terminal sessions rather than a GUI- or Electron-based client.

repos.name: morluto / rea
repos.description: Reverse engineer anything with agents, from app behavior down to native binaries.

summary.goal: REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) is an MCP server that connects coding agents or terminal commands to reverse-engineering tools for native binaries, JavaScript/Electron and .NET applications, and websites, returning evidence-backed findings.
summary.usage: Set up with `npx rea-agents setup`, choosing an agent and approving proposed MCP/config changes, then restart the agent. For CLI use, install globally with `npm install --global rea-agents` and run `rea --help`; Node.js 22.x (>=22.23.4), 24.x (>=24.22.1), or 26.12.1+ plus npm are required.
summary.pros: Analysis runs locally and each finding includes supporting evidence and stated limitations. REA covers a broad range of targets—native binaries, Go/Rust/EVM artifacts, Android APKs, .NET assemblies, firmware, and more—largely through built-in static inspection, and ships under the MIT license.
summary.cons: On Linux, several analysis paths (Ghidra, JADX, firmware tools, static JavaScript/Electron analysis) require a procps-compatible `ps` on REA's PATH for process-ownership checks, with documented recovery steps if missing. Deep native analysis also depends on separately obtained tools like Hopper, Ghidra, IDA, or Kuna.
summary.fit: REA appears suited for developers and researchers using coding agents to study software behavior for lawful research, education, interoperability, or preservation of software they own or are authorized to examine; commercial decompilers used alongside it (e.g., IDA Pro, Hopper) require their own separate licenses.

repos.name: Nutlope / hallmark
repos.description: Anti-AI-slop design skill for Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex.

summary.goal: Hallmark is a design skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode, made by Together AI and documented at https://www.usehallmark.com. It aims to generate web pages that avoid common visual tells associated with AI-generated design, applying a baseline of checks before building a page.
summary.usage: Install with `npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g`. Invoked harnesses can run commands such as `/hallmark redesign <path>` or `/hallmark audit <path>`, or a described build request, depending on the tool.
summary.pros: The project offers fifty selectable themes plus a custom design mode, dedicated redesign and audit commands, 755 openly licensed credited photographs, and an automated lint pass (sloplint) checking pages against known AI-style design tells.
summary.cons: The tool requires Node 18 or later, and its browser-based checks (such as rendering and screenshots) need an additional global install of puppeteer-core plus Chrome; without these, only static checks run.
summary.fit: Hallmark appears best suited to teams already using Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, or OpenCode, since it integrates as a skill or plugin within those harnesses rather than as a standalone application.

repos.name: thedotmack / claude-mem
repos.description: Persistent Context Across Sessions for Every Agent –  Captures everything your agent does during sessions, compresses it with AI, and injects relevant context back into future sessions. Works with Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex, Gemini, Hermes, Copilot, OpenCode + More

summary.goal: Claude-Mem gives coding agents persistent memory across sessions. A second 'observer' agent records notes while the primary agent works, so the next session opens with a compact index of prior observations instead of starting from zero.
summary.usage: Install with `npx claude-mem install` in an interactive terminal, or inside Claude Code run `/plugin marketplace add thedotmack/claude-mem` followed by `/plugin install claude-mem`; restart the agent afterward so new context loads automatically.
summary.pros: Search is organized as a token-efficient three-step MCP workflow (`search`, `timeline`, `get_observations`) said to give roughly 10x token savings versus fetching full details upfront, and any text wrapped in `<private>` tags is never stored.
summary.cons: Running `npm install -g claude-mem` installs only the SDK/library and does not register plugin hooks or start the worker service, so the documented path is `npx claude-mem install` or the `/plugin` commands instead; the tool also requires Node.js 20.19+ (20.x line) or 22.12+, with Bun and uv auto-installed if missing.
summary.fit: This seems suited for developers using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, or other supported coding agents who want memory to persist across sessions; it is released under the Apache License 2.0, which the README frames as chosen for easy embedding in developer tools and agent harnesses, though broader enterprise fit isn't detailed.

summary.goal: T3 Code is described as an "agent harness control surface" that lets users control coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx) running on their machine, accessible through iOS/Android apps, a web app, and an Electron-based desktop app.
summary.usage: Install via `curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh` (or the PowerShell equivalent on Windows), then run `t3` to start the server and open the local web app; `npx t3@latest` offers a one-time trial without installing.
summary.pros: Supports multiple existing agent subscriptions/providers and offers several install paths (winget, scoop, Homebrew, .deb, AUR, Nix) plus desktop, web, and mobile clients, with the project described as open so it can be forked if direction changes.
summary.cons: The README states the project is "very very early," warns users to expect bugs, and requires installing and authenticating at least one supported provider (e.g., Codex, Claude Code) before T3 Code can be used; it also says the project is mostly not accepting contributions yet.
summary.fit: Likely suited to developers already using one of the listed coding agents who want a unified, cross-device control interface; it may not fit users seeking a mature, stable tool or wanting to contribute large features, based on the README's early-stage caveats.

repos.name: heygen-com / hyperframes
repos.description: Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

summary.goal: HyperFrames is documented as a free, open-source framework for converting HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos. It can run locally via a CLI, be driven by AI coding agents through skills, or serve as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows.
summary.usage: A typical local workflow is `npx hyperframes init my-video`, then `cd my-video`, `npx hyperframes preview`, and `npx hyperframes render`, which requires Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg. For Claude Code, the README describes installing the plugin with `claude plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes` followed by `claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes`.
summary.pros: Documented strengths include HTML-native authoring with no React requirement, no build step for previewing an `index.html` composition, deterministic rendering where the same input yields the same frames, and an Apache 2.0 license with no per-render fees.
summary.cons: Cloning the full repository for development requires Git LFS, since golden regression-test baselines under `packages/producer/tests` include about 240 MB of `.mp4` files; a source-only clone can skip this content using `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1`.
summary.fit: The project appears best suited to teams or agents comfortable authoring in plain HTML/CSS who want deterministic, CI-friendly video rendering, since the README contrasts it with Remotion's React-based authoring model as the main difference between the two tools.

repos.name: pbakaus / impeccable
repos.description: The design vocabulary for your coding agent. Steer with polish and bolder, review with critique and audit, catch AI slop before it ships.

summary.goal: Impeccable is a design vocabulary toolkit for coding agents, providing commands like `polish`, `bolder`, `critique`, and `audit` to steer and review UI design and catch repetitive 'AI slop' patterns before shipping.
summary.usage: Install from a project root with `npx impeccable install`, then reload the coding tool and run `/impeccable init` (or `$impeccable init` on Codex) to set it up; afterward, commands such as `/impeccable critique the pricing cards` target specific components.
summary.pros: The detector uses 62 deterministic rules requiring no LLM or API key, works across many agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot, and others), and offers three ways to run checks: via an agent hook, CLI/CI, or a Chrome extension overlay.
summary.cons: Live mode's copy-edit 'Apply' feature can run the `codex` or `claude` CLI with approvals, permission checks, and sandboxing disabled while inheriting your environment, so reviewing this behavior before use in unfamiliar repos is advisable; some agents (Codex, Grok Build, Hermes Agent) also require a manual one-time hook-trust step.
summary.fit: The README states Impeccable works best on interfaces that already exist, for iterative, component-level review rather than building pages from scratch, and live mode integrates with dev servers for Vite, Next, SvelteKit, Astro, Nuxt, and plain HTML projects.

repos.name: HKUDS / DeepTutor
repos.description: DeepTutor: Lifelong Personalized Tutoring. https://deeptutor.info/.

summary.goal: DeepTutor is described as an agent-native learning workspace that connects tutoring, research, content creation, and practice in one extensible system, combining chat-based tutoring with knowledge-grounded retrieval and persistent memory.
summary.usage: Install via `python -m pip install -U "deeptutor[full]"`, then run `deeptutor init` to configure ports/provider and `deeptutor start` to launch backend and frontend (opens at http://127.0.0.1:3782 by default). A Docker image is also offered for a full-app trial.
summary.pros: Supports multiple retrieval engines (LlamaIndex, PageIndex, GraphRAG, LightRAG) selectable per knowledge base, offers an inspectable three-layer memory system (L1/L2/L3), and can connect live coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex as consultable subagents within a chat turn.
summary.cons: Authentication is off by default, meaning the application appears to run single-user unless an administrator manually enables it in `data/user/settings/auth.json` and configures per-user grants — shared deployments seem to require this extra setup step before being multi-user-ready.
summary.fit: Appears suited to individual learners or small teams wanting a self-hosted, extensible tutoring workspace; the PyPI/source installation path requires Python 3.11–3.14 and Node.js 20.9+, so those without a compatible runtime may prefer the Docker or desktop distributions instead.

repos.name: debpalash / VoiceStudio
repos.description: VoiceStudio is the open-source, fully-local ElevenLabs alternative — voice cloning, voice design, video dubbing, dictation, transcription & audiobook creation in 646 languages.

summary.goal: VoiceStudio is a locally run, AI-driven voice studio application documented as supporting voice cloning, voice design, video dubbing, dictation, transcription, and narration in 646 languages. The README states it runs on laptops, desktops, servers, phones, and tablets.
summary.usage: Installation differs by platform; documented examples include `brew install --cask debpalash/tap/voicestudio` on macOS, `curl -fsSL https://voicestudio.sh/install | sh` on macOS/Linux, and `git clone https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio.git` followed by `bun run dev` to run from source. After installing, the Get Started section describes opening the Voice cloning workspace, adding a reference recording, and generating speech; the app reportedly asks for confirmation before downloading any model.
summary.pros: The core desktop application is described as free, runs entirely on the user's own hardware, and needs no account. It is licensed under AGPL-3.0, which the README states covers commercial use under its terms, and offers many installation channels (Homebrew, AUR, Snap, DEB, AppImage, Docker, APK).
summary.cons: The README marks the Windows AMD ROCm setup as 'Experimental,' limited to selected RDNA2 RX 6000 GPUs (excluding the RX 6500 XT), which suggests GPU acceleration support may be inconsistent across AMD hardware configurations.
summary.fit: Given its emphasis on offline, on-device operation and its explicit requirement to clone a voice only with the owner's consent, VoiceStudio appears best suited to individual users or small teams wanting local voice generation rather than those needing hosted infrastructure, since the cloud offering (VoiceStudio Cloud) is still described as 'coming soon.'

repos.name: anthropics / claude-plugins-official
repos.description: Official, Anthropic-managed directory of high quality Claude Code Plugins.

summary.goal: This repository, anthropics/claude-plugins-official, is a curated directory of plugins for Claude Code, split into internally maintained plugins in /plugins and third-party plugins in /external_plugins.
summary.usage: Plugins are installed directly from this marketplace via Claude Code's plugin system, for example by running `/plugin install {plugin-name}@claude-plugins-official`, or by browsing entries through `/plugin > Discover`.
summary.pros: Each plugin follows a standard layout with a required plugin.json manifest plus optional .mcp.json configuration, commands, agents, and skills directories, and a plugin's `name` slug is treated as immutable so renames don't break existing installs.
summary.cons: The README states that Anthropic does not control the MCP servers, files, or other software bundled inside plugins and cannot verify they work as intended or won't change, so users are advised to trust a plugin before installing, updating, or using it.
summary.fit: The directory appears geared toward Claude Code users wanting a centralized way to find and install plugins, though the explicit trust-and-verification caveat suggests it may suit users comfortable independently vetting third-party plugin content.

repos.name: sherlock-project / sherlock
repos.description: Hunt down social media accounts by username across social networks

summary.goal: Sherlock is a command-line tool documented as helping users search for social media accounts tied to a specific username across 400+ social networks.
summary.usage: Installation can be done with `pipx install sherlock-project` (pip or uv are listed as alternatives), via Docker with `docker run -it --rm sherlock/sherlock`, or `dnf install sherlock-project`. To search, run `sherlock user123` for one username or `sherlock user1 user2 user3` for several; found accounts are saved to text files, and `sherlock --help` lists all available flags.
summary.pros: The README lists multiple installation routes (pipx/pip/uv, Docker, dnf), export options in CSV and XLSX formats, proxy support via `--proxy`, and flags for filtering specific sites, adjusting timeouts, and controlling output verbosity.
summary.cons: The documentation notes that third-party packages for ParrotOS and Ubuntu 24.04 are currently reported as broken, and that community-maintained packages for Debian, Ubuntu, Homebrew, Kali, and BlackArch are not directly supported or maintained by the Sherlock Project itself.
summary.fit: Based on the documented features, this tool may be best suited for OSINT-style username enumeration on systems with Python/pipx or Docker available; it is currently at version 0.16.0 and distributed under the MIT license.

repos.name: Leonxlnx / taste-skill
repos.description: Agent skills that give coding agents taste: art direction, reference images and a browser check instead of generic AI pages

summary.goal: Taste Skill (`tasteskill 2.5.1`) is an Agent Skill that directs coding agents to build professional company websites, aiming for a figma.com/x.ai level of design rather than generic landing pages, by enforcing rules such as one design system, real photographs and brand icons, and shader effects reserved for tech, gaming and software pages.
summary.usage: Install with `npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill --skill "design-taste-frontend"` using the npx skills CLI. Users then ask their coding agent to build or redesign a company site; the skill classifies the business type and runs scripts such as `node scripts/start.mjs deal --page software` from the project folder to deal layout tokens before the page is checked.
summary.pros: The skill verifies every build in a real headless-Chrome browser via a checker and finish gate before handing the page over, and it installs no extra dependencies or API keys itself, relying on bundled Wikimedia Commons photographs that work offline.
summary.cons: Running it requires Node 22+ and an installed Chrome, Edge or Chromium browser as a prerequisite, with ffmpeg only optional for WebP output; the finish gate caps automatic fixing at three rounds, so some flagged issues may plausibly remain unresolved if they are not fixable within that limit.
summary.fit: It appears best suited to teams already using agent-based coding tools like Claude Code or Codex, since it is distributed as a plugin/skill for those environments rather than a standalone web framework, and seems to favor company marketing/product sites over general-purpose application development.

repos.name: anthropics / knowledge-work-plugins
repos.description: Open source repository of plugins primarily intended for knowledge workers to use in Claude Cowork

summary.goal: Knowledge Work Plugins packages skills, connectors, slash commands, and sub-agents into 11 role-specific plugins (e.g., sales, finance, legal, data) that aim to turn Claude into a specialist for a given job function, built for Claude Cowork and also compatible with Claude Code.
summary.usage: Cowork users install plugins from claude.com/plugins/. Claude Code users first run `claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/knowledge-work-plugins`, then `claude plugin install sales@knowledge-work-plugins` (substituting the desired plugin); once installed, skills activate automatically and slash commands like `/sales:call-prep` become available.
summary.pros: Each plugin bundles domain skills that Claude draws on automatically, explicit slash commands, and MCP connectors to external tools; every component is file-based (markdown and JSON), requiring no code, infrastructure, or build steps.
summary.cons: The README describes these plugins as generic starting points that appear to become genuinely useful mainly after customization — editing `.mcp.json` for your tool stack and adding company-specific context to skill files — so out-of-the-box results may be limited until that setup is done.
summary.fit: Appears suited to teams or companies wanting to tailor Claude to their own tools, terminology, and processes across functions like sales, finance, legal, or data, using Claude Cowork or Claude Code.

repos.name: Vincentwei1021 / video-shotcraft
repos.description: AI video skill for Claude Code & Codex — cinematic, editable product promos with Remotion: 124 shot recipe cards, 150 motion previews, beat sync, sound design, Motion Workbench & JianYing (CapCut CN) export.

repos.name: AgriciDaniel / claude-seo
repos.description: Universal SEO skill for Claude Code. 26 sub-skills + 19 sub-agents covering technical SEO, E-E-A-T, schema, GEO/AEO, agent readiness (Lighthouse Agentic Browsing, WebMCP, llms.txt), backlinks, local SEO, e-commerce, international SEO, Google APIs, and PDF/Excel reporting. 9 optional extensions for live SEO data.

summary.goal: Claude SEO is described as a free, open-source SEO audit plugin for Claude Code, built from 26 sub-skills and 19 specialist agents, with up to 17 agents able to work in parallel. It runs a full site audit in 10 to 15 minutes covering technical SEO, Core Web Vitals, E-E-A-T, Schema.org structured data, AI search (GEO), and local/e-commerce SEO, producing a prioritized action plan.
summary.usage: Install inside Claude Code (version 1.0.33 or newer) by running /plugin marketplace add AgriciDaniel/claude-seo, /plugin install claude-seo@agricidaniel-claude-seo, and /seo setup. Afterward, commands such as /seo audit <url> run a full site audit.
summary.pros: The README states it is free under an MIT license with no per-site pricing or usage limits, runs locally so data stays on the user's own machine, applies the same checklist every time, and states its AI-search coverage follows Google's latest guidance.
summary.cons: Per the Requirements/Limits section, without Google API keys Core Web Vitals are lab estimates and indexing is inferred from the page rather than measured directly, and a full audit runs five agents on Opus, using more of a user's Claude plan than a single-page check.
summary.fit: The README states the project is built for SEO agencies wanting weekly client audits, in-house SEO teams at SaaS, publishing, and e-commerce companies, and freelance SEO consultants who want to show results on a first call.

repos.name: NationalSecurityAgency / ghidra
repos.description: Ghidra is a software reverse engineering (SRE) framework

summary.goal: Ghidra is a software reverse engineering (SRE) framework created and maintained by the NSA Research Directorate. It provides disassembly, assembly, decompilation, graphing, and scripting across Windows, macOS, and Linux, supporting a wide variety of processor instruction sets and executable formats.
summary.usage: Install JDK 25 64-bit, download an official release, extract it, then launch with ./ghidraRun (ghidraRun.bat on Windows) or the PyGhidra variant via ./support/pyghidraRun. To build from source instead, run gradle buildGhidra after fetching dependencies.
summary.pros: Ghidra runs in both user-interactive and automated modes and supports custom extensions and scripts written in Java or Python. It targets multiple platforms and processor architectures, and is distributed as an open source project with a public contributor process.
summary.cons: Certain Ghidra versions have known security vulnerabilities, so users are advised to review the published security advisories before deployment. Building from source also requires installing several separate toolchains, including JDK 25, Gradle 9.1.0+, Python3, and platform-specific compilers.
summary.fit: Ghidra is aimed at SRE analysts and teams handling complex, large-scale analysis efforts, including examining malicious code, and may suit users who need a customizable, extensible research platform rather than a lightweight single-purpose tool.
